normalized.description: Historical data associated with the uncontrolled re-entry of satellite and rocket bodies yielded that, as a rule of thumb, the driving uncertainty of where these events take place can be linked to 20% of the remaining orbital lifetime and that there is an underlying 50% uncertainty on the drag experienced between 80 and 200 km. These uncertainties are mostly empirical and neglect any relationwith the actual object shape and resulting drag, and feature as input to design for demise envelope condition when it comes to establishing fragmentation altitude and as such influence casualty risk reduction developments. Recently satellites have started to collect data and continue operation from 200km down to re-entry, allowing the investigation of said data from Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO)missions and the re-entry predictions of re-entry experiments to define a more realistic time windows for the re-entry epochs and dynamically accounting for (at least) the solar activity indexes. Linked to this initial uncertainty is the historical data on re-entry locations and debris found on-ground, to verify the accuracy of the on-ground impact probability for uncontrolled re-entry and the empirical correcting factors based on equatorial bulge and solar activity index. The activity aims to reduce the margins on uncertainties associated with initial break-ups during atmospheric destructive re-entry by recalibrating on data gathered from VLEO missions and re-entry experiments.
